clue.text: County bride's mega-rich pop

indicators.note: to pop is to burst, so the letters before it are blown apart and land in a new order

blocks.note: fourteen letters taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A local bride's enormously wealthy father, her pop, from the shires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' reads as the bride's dad, but it is the anagram signal. Cambridgeshire is an English county east of the Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambridgeshire is one of the English shire counties, home to the university city, so it is an example of a county.

clue.text: Is polite man a tax inspector?

definitions.text: Is polite man a tax inspector?

blocks.clueFragment: Is polite man a tax inspector?
blocks.note: surface reading: wondering whether a courteous gentleman works for the revenue
setter's reading: a courteous attendant, taken word by word, names the job of any government official

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, a 'polite' (civil) 'man' who serves is the phrase, and a tax inspector is exactly such a government employee.
explanation.definitionFit: Tax inspectors are employed by a government department, which makes each of them one of the state's salaried officials.

clue.text: Animals' cries heard

definitions.note: possessive in the surface; the answer is the plural noun

indicators.note: heard tells the solver to go by the sound of the word for cries, not its spelling

blocks.note: to mewl is to cry feebly, like a baby

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the noises animals make can be overheard.
explanation.definitionFit: Mules are hybrid farm beasts bred from a donkey and a horse, so they are examples of animals.

clue.text: Terse, sour nonconformist turned up

indicators.note: a nonconformist refuses the usual order, so these letters will not stay in theirs

blocks.note: nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A curt, sullen dissenter has arrived on the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' looks like 'arrived', but it describes a nose: retrousse, from French, is said of a snub nose that tilts upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrousse is the French-derived adjective for a nose whose tip tilts upward, so it means upturned.

clue.text: Rod and Eddy are confused and unsteady

indicators.note: confused things are muddled up, so the letters of the two names get mixed

blocks.note: the two names taken as written, the joining word left out

explanation.surface: Two men, Rod and Eddy, are muddled and wobbly on their feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Doddery describes someone, often elderly, who trembles and totters when walking, so it means shaky or unsteady.

clue.text: English reader discovering old German title

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
a lector is one who reads lessons aloud in church, or a university reader

explanation.surface: An English bookworm stumbles on an ancient German rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The princes who chose the Holy Roman Emperor held a historic German dignity carrying voting rights in the imperial election.

clue.text: Hurry in with a stethoscope

indicators.note: in says the letters wanted sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the run straddles the end of the first word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A doctor rushing in, stethoscope at the ready.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name speed of action or urgency, the noun for rushing to get something done quickly.

clue.text: Conservative has a good side

blocks.note: right as in correct or proper
a wing is a side section of a building or team

explanation.surface: A Tory politician turns out to have a decent streak.
explanation.definitionFit: Political parties of tradition and markets sit on the right of the spectrum, so a Tory belongs to that faction.

clue.text: King dismissed rogue servant

indicators.note: someone dismissed is sent away, so the royal letter is removed from the word that follows

blocks.note: R, from Latin rex, is the abbreviation for king
a varlet is an old word for a rascal or knave

explanation.surface: A monarch sacks a dishonest manservant.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the R out of VARLET to leave VALET; a varlet was originally a page or attendant too.
explanation.definitionFit: A valet is a gentleman's personal attendant who looks after his clothes, so he is a domestic servant.

clue.text: Address a gentleman about horse training

indicators.note: the words are read as being about, that is wrapped around, the run of letters wanted

blocks.note: the run spans the three words

explanation.surface: Speak to a gentleman on the subject of schooling horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is the equestrian discipline of training a horse to perform precise movements, so it is a form of schooling mounts.

clue.text: Starts to protest energetically about monarch, class and social hierarchy

indicators.note: starts means only the opening letters of the next two words are used

blocks.note: the opening letters of these two words
c, for circa, means about
a king is a monarch
an order is a rank or class, as in the lower orders

explanation.surface: Activists begin to rail loudly against the crown, the class system and society's ranking.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken from how hens rank themselves by pecking, the phrase names any informal ranking of status within a group.

clue.text: Liberal is a little pliant

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal
taken as written
some means a certain amount

explanation.surface: A politician of the Liberal party is somewhat flexible in their views.
explanation.definitionFit: Lissome describes a body that is slender and supple, bending gracefully, which matches flexible or supple.

clue.text: Mad Hatter first entertains the Royal Court, perhaps

indicators.note: mad means deranged, so the letters of the hat-maker's name are thrown out of order
first means only the opening letter of the following word is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Lewis Carroll's Mad Hatter is the first to amuse the king's court.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mad Hatter is from Alice in Wonderland, but 'Mad' works alone as the signal. The Royal Court is a London playhouse in Sloane Square.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Court in London is a famous playhouse staging new drama, so it is one example of a playhouse; perhaps flags that.

clue.text: Lear's unhappy noblemen

indicators.note: something unhappy is out of sorts, so the letters are put in a different order

blocks.note: the name taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's King Lear has miserable lords at his court.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls King Lear, whose earls of Kent and Gloucester suffer badly.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British peer ranking above viscount, so earls are members of the titled aristocracy.

clue.text: Oxide not often found on this planet?

blocks.note: rare means seldom occurring
the planet we live on

explanation.surface: A chemical compound seldom encountered anywhere in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a single question about scarcity, but it splits into a definition and two plain pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemists use the term for oxides of the lanthanide metals, which were once thought scarce; it now names those metals too.

clue.text: Standard police baton

blocks.note: the Yard is Scotland Yard, London's police headquarters
a baton is a short stick

explanation.surface: The truncheon a police officer is normally issued with.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard, often just 'the Yard', is the Metropolitan Police headquarters in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardstick is a measuring rod, and figuratively any benchmark against which things are judged.

clue.text: Hans and a girl set out to find paradise

indicators.note: to set out is to lay out afresh, so the letters are arranged anew

blocks.note: taken as written, the joining word left out

explanation.surface: A young couple head off on a quest for heaven on earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Shangri-La is the hidden Himalayan valley of bliss in James Hilton's novel Lost Horizon, now any earthly utopia.

clue.text: Mammal, perhaps, lacking one of these bones?

indicators.note: lacking means something is missing, so a letter must be taken away

blocks.note: a mammal is one kind of backboned animal; perhaps marks it as an example
one of the word's two Ts goes, the second

explanation.surface: Could a mammal be missing one of its spinal bones?
explanation.walkthrough: VERTEBRATE has two Ts; drop one, the second, and VERTEBRAE remains. The joke is that a vertebrate is defined by having these bones.
explanation.definitionFit: Vertebrae are the small linked bones that make up the spinal column, the plural of vertebra.

clue.text: Said to be fundamental part of seed

indicators.note: said means the word is spoken, so a word that sounds the same is wanted

blocks.note: radical means going to the root, basic

explanation.surface: A botanist claims to have found the essential component of a seed.
explanation.definitionFit: The radicle is the embryonic root, the first portion of a seedling to emerge from a germinating seed.

clue.text: Ms Mabel Wild prepares for funeral

indicators.note: wild means unruly, so the letters run riot into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman called Mabel Wild gets ready for a burial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' looks like Mabel's surname, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To embalm is to treat a corpse with preservatives to delay decay, a step in readying a body before burial.

clue.text: Gas makes one groan in distress

indicators.note: something in distress is in a bad way, so its letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wind or indigestion leaves a person moaning in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gas' suggests wind and discomfort, but it is a chemical element here.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is an inert element found in air, one of the noble gases.

clue.text: Irritated Spike and Penny

blocks.note: a needle is a sharp point or spike
d, from Latin denarius, was the old abbreviation for a penny

explanation.surface: Two people, Spike and Penny, are annoyed with each other.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike and Penny look like names. D stood for a penny in Britain's pre-1971 money.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to provoke or annoy them persistently, so needled means annoyed.

clue.text: Break from playing lute and piano

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are played around with into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A musician takes a rest from strumming the lute and playing the keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-up is a pause or easing off in some activity, which is a respite or interval.

clue.text: Imaginary monster insect with a frightening cry

blocks.note: a bug is an insect
taken as written
boo is what you shout to startle someone

explanation.surface: A make-believe beast, a creepy-crawly that shrieks to scare people.
explanation.definitionFit: A bugaboo is a bogeyman, an object of dread conjured up to scare children, so it is a fancied beast.

clue.text: Colonel and bishop walk unsteadily

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
to limp is to walk lamely

explanation.surface: An army officer and a cleric totter along together.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel Blimp was a pompous cartoon officer by David Low, whose name now stands for any reactionary diehard.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonel Blimp is the cartoon character, so the surname fills out the title just as a name follows a rank.

clue.text: Reviewer's heartless, antisocial and uncomplimentary

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle of the next word is removed, leaving its outside

blocks.note: a critic reviews books, plays or films
only the first and last letters are kept

explanation.surface: A cold, unfriendly reviewer writes a damning notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Critical remarks express disapproval and find fault, so they are the opposite of flattering.

clue.text: I upset Dali. (It's a long story!)

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the painter's name taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone offended Salvador Dali, and explaining how would take a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a long story' is the stock phrase for avoiding explanation, but here it literally defines an epic.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's Iliad is an epic poem of the Trojan War running to over fifteen thousand lines, a lengthy narrative indeed.

clue.text: He steals fish, the cheeky lad

blocks.note: to whip is slang for to steal, so one who does it
a snapper is a tropical food fish

explanation.surface: The impudent boy is a thief who pinches fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A whippersnapper is a young person thought presumptuous or overconfident, which fits an impudent youngster.
